title: The King Rejoices in Your Strength
summary: The people give thanks that God has granted the king his heart's desire: a crown of gold, long life, glory, and joy in God's presence. Because the king trusts in the LORD and in his loving devotion, he will not be shaken. The second half looks ahead to God's victory over all his enemies, pictured as a consuming fire, and the psalm closes with a call for the LORD to be exalted in his strength.
story: Psalm 21 is the companion to Psalm 20. There the people prayed that God would give the king his heart's desire and grant his petitions; here they thank God that he has done exactly that (compare 20:4 with 21:2). Together the two psalms form a before and after around the king's day of trouble. Coming just before Psalm 22, the great cry of the abandoned sufferer, Psalm 21 shows the king crowned, blessed, and secure. The next psalm shows the depths. Read in sequence, the Psalter holds the royal glory and the royal suffering side by side, a pairing Christians have found full of meaning.
historical:
The heading is the same as Psalm 20: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. Traditional readers see David giving thanks for his own victories or for the covenant blessings of 2 Samuel 7. Many modern scholars treat it as a liturgy for a Davidic king, perhaps used after a battle, on a coronation day, or at an anniversary of the king's accession; the mention of a crown of pure gold in verse 3 has led some to connect it with a coronation. The text doesn't settle the question, and it may have served on more than one kind of occasion.

Later Jewish tradition read the king of this psalm as the Messiah. The Targum, the ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Scriptures used in the synagogue, renders the king of verses 1 and 7 as King Messiah. Its date is debated (it reached its final form well after the time of Jesus), but it shows that Jewish readers, too, heard in the royal psalms a hope that reached beyond any king who had yet reigned.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern courts addressed kings in the language of eternity. Israel shared the formula: Bathsheba says to David, May my lord King David live forever (1 Kings 1:31), and Nehemiah greets the Persian king the same way (Nehemiah 2:3). So when verse 4 says the king asked for life and received length of days forever and ever, a first reader would hear court language, a prayer for a long reign and an enduring dynasty. In Israel it carried extra weight because God had promised David a house and throne established forever (2 Samuel 7:16).

The fiery furnace of verse 9 translates a word for an oven, the clay bread oven found in almost every ancient household, heated until it glowed. The image is of total and swift destruction. Destroying an enemy's descendants, as verse 10 says, meant ending a hostile royal line so that it could not rise again, a grim reality of ancient warfare, here pictured as God's own judgment.
literary: The psalm is a royal thanksgiving in two panels framed by the same phrase, in Your strength (verses 1 and 13). The first panel (verses 1 to 7) speaks to God about the king in the third person, listing the gifts God has given him: heart's desire, blessings, a crown, life, glory, splendor, joy. Verse 7 is the hinge, stating the reason: the king trusts in the LORD and in the loving devotion of the Most High. The second panel (verses 8 to 12) turns to address the king, or perhaps God (the Hebrew allows either), promising the defeat of every enemy. Verse 13 closes with the whole congregation's praise. The word Selah after verse 2, found seventy-one times in the Psalms, is of uncertain meaning; it may mark a musical interlude or a pause.

outline.t: Thanksgiving for the gifts God has given the king
The king trusts in the LORD's loving devotion
The coming defeat of every enemy
Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength

doctrines.note: Every gift the king enjoys, from his crown to his life, is received from God. The psalm presents Israel's king as a dependent of the divine King, whose strength is the real power in the land.
Verses 8 to 12 describe God's final victory over those who plot evil against him. The enemies are God's enemies (those who hate You), and the judgment is his, not the king's private revenge.
The king's security rests on God's loving devotion (verse 7), the steadfast covenant love promised to David's house in 2 Samuel 7.

words.note: Yeshu'ah, salvation, deliverance, victory. In a military setting it can mean simply a rescue or a win in battle, and it frames the king's joy in verses 1 and 5. The name Jesus (Yeshua) comes from the same root, meaning the LORD saves.

Batach, to trust, to feel secure in something. The Psalms use it again and again for where a person rests his weight. In verse 7 it is the hinge of the whole psalm: the king is blessed not because he is strong but because he trusts.
Elyon, Most High. An old title for God, used by Melchizedek king of Salem when he blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18-20). It presents God as supreme over every power, the king above all kings.
Atarah, crown. The word can mean a royal crown, a wreath, or any headdress of honor. A crown of pure gold marks the king's authority as a gift placed on his head by God, not a prize he took.

christ: The psalm pictures a king who asks God for life and receives length of days forever, and who is given glory, splendor, and joy in God's presence. No king of Judah lived forever; their line ended in exile. The early church read such language as fulfilled in Jesus, whom God raised from the dead to reign forever at his right hand. Hebrews speaks of Jesus as crowned with glory and honor after suffering death (Hebrews 2:9), and Revelation pictures him wearing many crowns (Revelation 19:12). The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 21 directly, so this is a reading of its pattern and hope rather than a stated prophecy. The placement of the psalm next to Psalm 22 has struck Christian readers as fitting: the crown and the cross belong together in the story of the Messiah.

hard.q: How should a reader handle the psalm's picture of enemies burned in a furnace and their descendants wiped from the earth?
hard.a: The language is severe and belongs to the vocabulary of ancient warfare, where victory over a hostile dynasty often meant its end. Several things keep it in perspective. The enemies are defined as those who hate God and plot evil against him (verses 8 and 11), and the action belongs to God, not to the king's private vengeance. The fire is a common biblical image of divine judgment, not a description of a literal execution method. Some interpreters read these verses chiefly as a prophetic picture of God's final judgment on evil; others emphasize their original setting in Israel's wars and argue that Christians should read them in light of Jesus' command to love enemies, praying for justice while leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19). Both approaches agree that the psalm is not a license for human cruelty.

questions: The king's gifts all come from God. What in your life have you been tempted to treat as your own achievement rather than a gift received?
Verse 7 says the king will not be shaken because he trusts in God's loving devotion. What shakes you most easily, and what would it look like to rest your weight elsewhere?
How do you read the psalm's language of judgment alongside Jesus' call to love your enemies?
